abstracts.abstract: We present a novel probabilistic framework for analyzing graph degeneracy that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between graph structure and algorithmic tractability. Traditional approaches treat degeneracy as a static parameter; our framework introduces random sampling dynamics that reveal structural properties previously obscured by worst-case analysis. We establish that for any graph G with average degree d, the expected degeneracy under our sampling procedure equals Θ(d/log d), significantly deviating from classical bounds. This leads to new connections between probabilistic methods and combinatorial optimization. Our main theorem demonstrates that the probabilistic degeneracy framework provides a unifying perspective on several seemingly disparate problems in extremal combinatorics, including forbidden subgraph characterization and independence number estimation. We further show that this framework yields novel insights into additive combinatorics through its application to sum-product phenomena in sparse graphs. The paradigm shift enabled by our approach suggests that probabilistic sampling should be considered a fundamental tool in graph theory, not merely an analytical technique. Computational experiments on large-scale network data confirm theoretical predictions, establishing the practical viability of the probabilistic paradigm.

We establish significantly improved bounds on classical Ramsey-type results concerning forbidden subgraphs in dense graphs. While the celebrated Ramsey number R(3,k) has been extensively studied, we focus on asymmetric Ramsey phenomena involving bipartite forbidden configurations. Our main contribution is a substantial improvement to the best-known upper bounds for mixed Ramsey numbers involving odd cycles and complete bipartite graphs. Using an enhanced application of the probabilistic method combined with novel iterative density increment arguments, we prove that for sufficiently large n, any graph on n vertices with more than n^(5/3)/2 edges contains either a triangle-free subgraph with independence number exceeding n^(2/5) or a specific forbidden bipartite structure. This result improves upon the previous best known bounds by a factor of n^(1/15) in the extremal setting. Furthermore, we extend our techniques to address analogous questions in combinatorial number theory, establishing improved bounds for Schur-type Ramsey problems in sparse sets. The methods developed herein represent a refined application of probabilistic and extremal techniques that should prove useful in other contexts involving forbidden subgraph problems. Our work resolves open questions posed in the literature regarding the precise asymptotic behavior of these Ramsey-type functions.

We introduce a novel algorithmic framework for solving connectivity problems in large-scale networks that fundamentally differs from classical approaches based on spanning trees or augmenting paths. Our framework, grounded in matroid theory and combinatorial geometry, treats network connectivity as a geometric optimization problem in the graphic matroid space. The key innovation lies in representing network flows as points in a high-dimensional space, enabling the application of convex optimization techniques to discrete combinatorial problems. We present algorithms for minimum cut, maximum flow, and connectivity verification that achieve O(m^(4/3)) expected time complexity for general networks with m edges, matching or improving upon the best known deterministic bounds. Our approach provides a unified treatment of several previously disparate problems in algorithmic graph theory, including Gomory-Hu trees, minimum cost flows, and multiway cuts. The geometric perspective reveals structural properties previously unnoticed, leading to natural parallelization strategies with near-linear speedup on standard architectures. Extensive computational experiments on real-world network datasets demonstrate that our framework scales effectively to networks with millions of vertices while maintaining theoretical performance guarantees. This work opens new directions for applying continuous optimization methods to discrete structures.

We develop a significantly faster algorithm for computing maximum flows in networks with integral capacities, addressing a central problem in combinatorial optimization with extensive applications in network theory. Our algorithm achieves O(m^(3/2)) time complexity for general networks, improving upon the previous best bound of O(m n^(2/3)) by a factor of n^(2/3)/m^(1/2) in dense graphs. The improvement stems from a novel combination of blocking flow techniques with dynamic tree data structures that more efficiently exploit graph structure during the augmenting phase. We introduce the concept of locally sparse residual networks, which allow us to maintain and update augmenting paths with substantially reduced overhead. Our approach achieves particularly strong performance on practical networks exhibiting community structure, with empirical running times significantly better than theoretical predictions. We provide a complete implementation with careful engineering for cache-efficient memory access patterns, achieving near-linear scaling on multi-core processors. The algorithm maintains flexibility to handle both small integral capacities and large real-valued capacities through parameter-dependent specializations. Applications to transportation networks and communication systems demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, with speedups of 3-10x observed compared to state-of-the-art implementations on benchmark instances.
